abstract: Sigelman, Fuller, Fenlon, Leiden and Guilford argue that generative AI's central labor market effect is not on the number of jobs but on the level of expertise required to do them, and that the decisive variable is the shape of an occupation's learning curve. Where expertise accrues gradually through experience, mentorship and progressively harder work - what the authors call Growth Roles - GenAI automates precisely the foundational tasks that historically served as the training ground, narrowing the entry point and eroding the pipeline. Where expertise is front-loaded as a body of codified technical knowledge mastered at the outset - Mastery Roles - GenAI compresses the time to initial proficiency and widens access. The authors identify 273 highly impacted occupations employing almost 50 million US workers and split them across these two archetypes: 17.8 million workers (about 12% of the labor force) in Growth Roles facing narrowed entry, and 28.6 million (roughly 19%) in Mastery Roles facing lowered barriers. The distributional sting is that the narrowing side is the better-paid side: Growth Roles pay 28% more on average, a $20,000 annual difference, and are 51% more likely to require a college degree, so the authors conclude that AI will disproportionately restrict entry points to high-value careers. The organizational implication they draw is a shift from pyramid-shaped talent models with broad junior bases toward flatter, diamond-shaped structures, with firms moving emphasis from talent acquisition to retention of scarce expertise.
keyFindings: 273 occupations identified as highly impacted by GenAI, together employing almost 50 million US workers - roughly 31% of the labor force when the two archetype shares are combined.

Growth Roles: approximately 1 in 8 US workers (17.8 million people, about 12% of the labor force) are in occupations where there could be considerably less entry-level opportunity as a result of GenAI. Examples given are legal associates, marketing specialists, and project managers.

Mastery Roles: about 1 in 5 workers (28.6 million people, roughly 19% of the workforce) are in fields where GenAI could take on technically sophisticated tasks, reducing hard-skills requirements and expanding access. Examples are network administrators, data warehousing specialists, and loan interviewers.

Growth Roles pay 28% more on average than Mastery Roles - a difference of $20,000 annually - and are 51% more likely to require a college degree. The authors conclude AI 'will disproportionately restrict entry points to high-value careers.'
Mastery Roles currently employ 11 million more workers than Growth Roles, so the larger population sees the access-widening effect while the higher-paid population sees the narrowing effect.

The mechanism is explicitly about learning curves, not task counts: in Growth Roles 'GenAI automates foundational work that historically served as the training ground for future expertise,' while in Mastery Roles it 'acts as an equalizer, compressing the time required to gain initial proficiency.'

Organizational forecast: pyramid-shaped talent models with broad junior bases give way to flatter, diamond-shaped structures, which may speed information exchange but create fewer opportunities to accrue management experience. Firms shift from acquisition to retention of scarce expertise.
methodology: Analysis of Lightcast US job postings data for the prior two years, which the authors state includes over 99% of jobs posted online during that timeframe. GenAI itself is used to assess the knowledge required in each occupation, building on existing models of LLM task impacts. Each role's learning curve is mapped from the productivity increase implied by typical compensation growth across the tenure distribution - the steeper the pay progression with experience, the more back-loaded the learning curve. A series of projection models then estimates GenAI's likely effects on the skills required in each occupation and their relative importance, separately for entry-level versus higher-level job openings. Occupations are screened first for significant GenAI impact (yielding the 273), then classified as Growth or Mastery by learning-curve shape. Employment levels and wages are drawn from US labor market data for the occupations as they exist today. A joint product of the Burning Glass Institute and the Harvard Business School Project on Managing the Future of Work, distributed through the Harvard Kennedy School Project on Workforce.
qualifiers: Tier 2: industry/think-tank research, not peer-reviewed. The headline figures are projections about which occupations will be affected, not measured outcomes - the authors are explicit that the analysis 'focuses on which types of occupations are likely to bear the brunt of AI automation, and not on the potential impact of AI on employment levels.' So neither the 17.8 million nor the 28.6 million is a count of jobs lost or gained; both are counts of workers in occupations whose entry dynamics are expected to change. The authors list their own limitations directly: 'uncertainty about GenAI's future capabilities and the speed of adoption make it hard to forecast the magnitude and timing of its impact'; their five-year automation and augmentation projection 'suggests that the timing of such changes could take place sooner - or, perhaps, over a much longer period'; the report covers only LLM capabilities involving text and images and 'doesn't assess the potential impact of other AI capabilities such as robotics or specialized domain models'; it 'considers only the skills, wages, employment levels, and occupations of today' without modeling how those evolve apart from GenAI; and it estimates 'the impact of automation from GenAI alone.' The learning-curve inference is indirect - curve shape is read off compensation growth by tenure, which conflates returns to experience with seniority premiums, selection into higher-paying firms, and internal pay norms. Occupation classification is performed by an LLM, so the treatment variable is itself model-generated. Findings are US-based; the authors note the underlying skill patterns may generalize but 'the net workforce impacts could differ widely based on the considerable variance in the distribution of occupations across economies.' Note also a minor internal inconsistency: the executive summary rounds Mastery Roles to 'twenty-nine million' while the body text gives 28.6 million.
